title: No. 42 — The Powers Conferred by the Constitution Further Considered (Madison)
paragraphs: The SECOND class of powers placed in the general government consists of those that govern dealings with foreign nations. These are: to make treaties; to send and receive ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls; to define and punish piracies and felonies committed on the high seas, and offenses against the law of nations; and to regulate foreign commerce. The last includes a power to prohibit, after the year 1808, the importation of slaves, and to lay in the meantime a duty of ten dollars per head, to discourage such importations.
These powers are an obvious and essential part of federal administration. If we are to be one nation in anything, we should plainly be one in relation to other nations.

The powers to make treaties and to send and receive ambassadors are obviously proper and need no defense. Both are already in the articles of Confederation, with only two differences. First, the Convention's plan removes from the treaty power an exception under which treaties could be largely defeated by regulations of the States. Second, a power of appointing and receiving "other public ministers and consuls" is expressly added, and rightly so, to the earlier provision about ambassadors. Taken strictly, as the second of the articles of Confederation seems to require, the term ambassador covers only the highest rank of public ministers. It leaves out the ranks that the United States will most likely prefer wherever foreign embassies are needed. And no stretching of the term can make it cover consuls. Yet Congress has found it useful, and has made a practice of it, to employ the lower ranks of public ministers and to send and receive consuls.

It is true that where commercial treaties provide for each side to appoint consuls whose functions relate to commerce, admitting foreign consuls may fall within the power of making commercial treaties. It is also true that where there are no such treaties, sending American consuls to foreign countries may PERHAPS be covered by the authority given in the ninth article of the Confederation to appoint all civil officers needed to manage the general affairs of the United States. But admitting consuls into the United States where no earlier treaty has so provided seems not to have been provided for anywhere. Filling this gap is one of the smaller ways in which the Convention has improved on the model it had before it. Yet even the smallest provisions matter when they remove the need, or the excuse, for gradual and unnoticed usurpations of power. A list of the cases in which the defects of the Confederation have betrayed or forced Congress into violating its chartered authority would greatly surprise anyone who has not paid attention to the subject. It would also be a considerable argument for the new Constitution, which seems to have attended as carefully to the lesser defects of the old system as to the more obvious and striking ones.

The power to define and punish piracies and felonies committed on the high seas, and offenses against the law of nations, belongs just as properly to the general government, and is a still greater improvement on the articles of Confederation. Those articles make no provision for offenses against the law of nations. As a result, any careless member can embroil the Confederacy with foreign nations. On piracies and felonies, the federal articles go no further than establishing courts to try these offenses. The definition of piracies might perhaps be left to the law of nations without harm, though most municipal codes do contain a legislative definition of them. A definition of felonies on the high seas is clearly needed. Felony is a loosely defined term even in the common law of England, and it has varied meanings in that kingdom's statute law. But neither the common law nor the statute law of England, or of any other nation, ought to be the standard for our proceedings unless our legislature has first adopted it as its own. The meaning of the term as defined in the codes of the individual States would be an impractical guide, just as the English law would be a dishonorable and illegitimate one. It is not exactly the same in any two States, and in each of them it changes with every revision of its criminal laws. For the sake of certainty and uniformity, then, the power to define felonies in this case was in every respect necessary and proper.

The regulation of foreign commerce has been taken up from several points of view in earlier discussion of this subject. It has been discussed too fully to need more proof here that it is properly placed in the federal administration.

It is certainly to be wished that the power to prohibit the importation of slaves had not been postponed until 1808, or rather that it had been allowed to take effect at once. But it is not hard to explain either this restriction on the general government or the way the whole clause is worded. We should count it a great point won for humanity that within twenty years this traffic, which has so long and so loudly reproached the barbarism of modern policy, may be ended forever within these States. In that time the federal government will discourage it considerably, and the few States that continue the unnatural traffic may agree to abolish it entirely, following the example of prohibition set by so great a majority of the Union. How happy it would be for the unfortunate Africans if they had an equal prospect of being redeemed from the oppressions of their European brethren!

Some have tried to turn this clause into an objection to the Constitution. On one side it is portrayed as a criminal tolerance of an illicit practice, and on another as likely to prevent voluntary and beneficial emigration from Europe to America. I mention these misreadings not to answer them, since they deserve no answer, but as samples of the manner and spirit in which some have chosen to carry on their opposition to the proposed government.
The powers in the THIRD class are those that provide for harmony and proper dealings among the States.

The particular restraints placed on the authority of the States, and certain powers of the judicial department, might be included under this head. But the former are set aside for a class of their own, and the latter will be examined in detail when we come to the structure and organization of the government. I will limit myself to a quick review of the remaining powers that fall under this third description. They are: to regulate commerce among the several States and the Indian tribes; to coin money, and to regulate its value and the value of foreign coin; to provide for the punishment of counterfeiting the current coin and securities of the United States; to fix the standard of weights and measures; to establish a uniform rule of naturalization and uniform laws of bankruptcy; to prescribe how the public acts, records and judicial proceedings of each State shall be proved, and what effect they shall have in other States; and to establish post offices and post roads.

The existing Confederacy's lack of power to regulate commerce among its members is one of the defects that experience has clearly exposed. To the proofs and remarks that earlier papers have offered on this subject we can add that, without this supplementary provision, the great and essential power of regulating foreign commerce would have been incomplete and ineffective. One very important aim of this power was to relieve the States that import and export through other States from the improper contributions those other States levy on them. If the latter were free to regulate trade between one State and another, we must foresee that they would find ways to burden articles of import and export, while passing through their territory, with duties that would fall on the producers of the exports and the consumers of the imports. Past experience assures us that such a practice would be brought in by future schemes. Both that experience and common knowledge of human affairs assure us that it would feed endless animosities and might well end in serious breaches of the public peace. For those who do not look at the question through passion or self-interest, the desire of the commercial States to collect, in any form, an indirect revenue from their uncommercial neighbors must seem as unwise as it is unfair, because resentment as well as interest would drive the injured party to look for less convenient channels for its foreign trade. But the mild voice of reason, pleading for a broader and lasting interest, is all too often drowned out, in public bodies as well as in individuals, by the clamor of an impatient greed for immediate and excessive gain.

Other examples besides our own have shown the need for an authority overseeing the mutual trade of confederated States. In Switzerland, where the Union is very loose, each canton must let merchandise pass through its territory into other cantons without raising the tolls. In Germany it is a law of the empire that the princes and states may not lay tolls or customs on bridges, rivers or passages without the consent of the emperor and the diet. But a quotation in an earlier paper shows that in this matter, as in many others in that confederacy, practice has not followed the law, and has produced there the harms we have foreseen here. Among the restraints the Union of the Netherlands puts on its members is one that they may not establish imposts disadvantageous to their neighbors without general permission.

It is quite right that the regulation of commerce with the Indian tribes is freed from two limits in the articles of Confederation, which make the provision there obscure and contradictory. There the power is confined to Indians who are not members of any of the States, and it must not violate or infringe the legislative right of any State within its own limits. Which Indians are to count as members of a State has not been settled, and it has often caused perplexity and contention in the federal councils. And how trade with Indians who are not members of a State but live within its legislative jurisdiction can be regulated by an outside authority, without intruding on the State's internal rights of legislation, is simply incomprehensible. This is not the only case where the articles of Confederation have thoughtlessly tried to accomplish impossibilities: to reconcile a partial sovereignty in the Union with complete sovereignty in the States, and to overturn a mathematical axiom by taking away a part and leaving the whole.

All that needs saying about the power to coin money, and to regulate its value and that of foreign coin, is that by providing for foreign coin the Constitution has filled a significant gap in the articles of Confederation. The authority of the existing Congress is limited to regulating coin STRUCK by its own authority or by that of the respective States. It is plain at once that the planned uniformity in the VALUE of the current coin could be destroyed if foreign coin were left to the different regulations of the different States.
Punishing the counterfeiting of public securities, as well as of the current coin, naturally goes to the authority that is to secure the value of both.
The regulation of weights and measures is carried over from the articles of Confederation, and rests on the same considerations as the preceding power to regulate coin.

The differences among the States in the rules of naturalization have long been noted as a fault in our system, and as a basis for intricate and delicate questions. The fourth article of the Confederation declares "that the FREE INHABITANTS of each of these States, paupers, vagabonds, and fugitives from justice, excepted, shall be entitled to all privileges and immunities of FREE CITIZENS in the several States; and THE PEOPLE of each State shall, in every other, enjoy all the privileges of trade and commerce," etc. The language here is remarkably confused. It is hard to tell why the terms FREE INHABITANTS are used in one part of the article, FREE CITIZENS in another and PEOPLE in another, or what was meant by adding "all the privileges of trade and commerce" to "all privileges and immunities of free citizens." It seems nearly unavoidable, though, to conclude that those who count as FREE INHABITANTS of a State, even if not citizens of that State, are entitled in every other State to all the privileges of FREE CITIZENS of that other State. That means greater privileges than they may have in their own State. So a particular State may have the power, or rather every State is placed under a necessity, to confer the rights of citizenship in other States, not only on anyone it admits to such rights within itself, but on anyone it allows to become an inhabitant within its jurisdiction. But suppose we accepted an interpretation of the term "inhabitants" that confined the promised privileges to citizens alone. The difficulty would only be reduced, not removed. Each State would still keep the very improper power of naturalizing aliens in every other State. In one State a short residence confers all the rights of citizenship, and in another more important qualifications are required. So an alien who is legally barred from certain rights in the latter State may get around the bar merely by having lived earlier in the former. In this way the law of one State is absurdly made to override the law of another within that other State's own jurisdiction. We owe it to mere chance that we have so far escaped very serious embarrassments over this. By the laws of several States, certain kinds of aliens who had made themselves obnoxious were put under prohibitions that were inconsistent not only with the rights of citizenship but with the privilege of residence. What would have followed if such persons, by residence or otherwise, had acquired the character of citizens under the laws of another State, and had then claimed their rights as citizens, both to residence and to citizenship, in the State that had banned them? Whatever the legal consequences might have been, other consequences would probably have followed that were too serious not to be guarded against. The new Constitution has accordingly, and very properly, made provision against them, and against all other consequences of the Confederation's defect on this point, by authorizing the general government to establish a uniform rule of naturalization throughout the United States.

The power to establish uniform laws of bankruptcy is so closely tied to the regulation of commerce, and will prevent so many frauds where the parties or their property may be located or moved in different States, that its usefulness seems unlikely to be questioned.

The power to prescribe, by general laws, how the public acts, records and judicial proceedings of each State shall be proved, and what effect they shall have in other States, is a clear and valuable improvement on the corresponding clause in the articles of Confederation. The meaning of that clause is extremely vague, and under any reading it will bear it can matter very little. The power established here may become a very convenient instrument of justice. It will be especially useful on the borders of neighboring States, where property that is liable to legal process may be quickly and secretly moved into a foreign jurisdiction at any stage of the proceeding.

The power of establishing post roads must in every view be harmless, and with sound management may perhaps become the source of great public convenience. Nothing that helps the intercourse between the States can be thought unworthy of the public's attention.
